name: Gilt (gold leaf laid over a substrate)

appliesTo.note: Gilt is a working, not a substance (D-014): gold leaf about a tenth of a micrometre thick, laid over plaster, bronze or wood. The appearance is the leaf's; wear shows what lies under it. The white and oak groups name their plaster and timber substances; gilt applies to them by family.

process: Gold is alloyed to 23.75 carat, rolled and beaten between skins until a leaf is about 0.1 um thick, and cut into leaves of about 80 mm. The gilder lays it by one of two methods. Water gilding (for carved wood, frames and fine interior work): six to twelve coats of gesso (chalk or gypsum in rabbit-skin glue) are laid and smoothed, then four to eight coats of bole (a fine clay, red, yellow or blue-grey, in glue); the bole is wetted with gilder's liquor, the leaf is floated on, and when dry the gold is burnished with an agate to a mirror, or left matte, the two set side by side. Oil gilding (for plaster, metal and architectural work): a drying-oil size is brushed on and the leaf laid when the size is just tacky; it cannot be burnished and has a softer lustre. On bronze the historic method was fire gilding with a mercury amalgam, now abandoned for its danger; the museum's gilt bronze is oil gilt.

tarnish.text: The 23-23.75 kt leaves carry no tarnishing risk, and the 23.75 kt leaf is recommended for exteriors; the risk rises as the carat falls (low for most 22-23 kt alloys, high for 16-18 kt green golds, very high for white golds).
tarnish.source: Giusto Manetti Battiloro, French cut leaf, alloy table (tarnishing risk per alloy: 'NO RISK' for orange gold 23.75 kt and 23.5 kt, florin and yellow extra 23 kt; 'HIGH RISK' for green gold 18 kt and pale gold 16 kt; 'VERY HIGH RISK' for the white golds; 23.75 kt 'RECOMMENDED FOR EXTERIORS'), https://www.manetti.com/en/product/french-cut-leaf/

opacity.text: The leaf is optically thick. Light entering gold decays to 1/e in 14-21 nm across the visible, so a 100 nm leaf passes about 0.1-0.9 % of the light that enters it, most near 500 nm (why thin gold looks green by transmitted light). Reflection from the leaf is that of bulk gold; nothing of the substrate shows through an intact leaf.

f0.derivation: Unpolarised Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence, R = ((n-1)^2 + k^2) / ((n+1)^2 + k^2), from the tabulated n,k interpolated linearly to 380-780 nm in 10 nm steps (end values held), integrated against the CIE 1931 2-degree colour-matching functions under CIE illuminant D65, normalised so that a perfect reflector has Y = 1, and converted from XYZ to linear Rec.709 with the sRGB matrix. value: Babar and Weaver 2015 (the most recent of the three). Johnson and Christy 1972: [1.037, 0.729, 0.364]. Rioux et al. 2014 pure Au (the model's 1 nm table, sampled like the others): [1.055, 0.779, 0.335]. min and max are the channel-by-channel envelope of the three.

alloyEffect.text: Ten per cent silver moves gold's F0 from [1.055, 0.779, 0.335] to [1.001, 0.819, 0.375] (Rioux et al. 2014 Au and Au90Ag10, same method): red down 0.05, green and blue up 0.04. The leaf's ~1 % of silver and copper moves it by about a tenth of that, below the spread between the measured datasets.
alloyEffect.derivation: F0 of Rioux's Au and Au90Ag10 computed as for f0 and compared; scaling the change by one tenth for a 1 % addition assumes it is linear in silver content at small additions.

burnish.text: When the gilding has dried, it is burnished with a polished agate: the springy bole under the leaf lets the stone compress the gold into a true mirror. Burnished and matte areas are set side by side.

methods.text: An amalgam of gold and mercury is applied to copper, brass or bronze and heated until the mercury evaporates, leaving a gold film that retains 13-16 % mercury. The fumes cause serious illness; France legislated against it around 1830, and it has been replaced by electroplating. It is recorded here because historic gilt bronze was made this way; the museum does not imitate it.

mercuryRetained.source: Wikipedia, 'Gilding' (fire-gilding leaves 'a film of gold or an amalgam containing 13 to 16% mercury', its ref. 3), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilding

abandoned.source: Wikipedia, 'Ormolu' ('Around 1830, legislation in France outlawed the use of mercury for health reasons, though use continued to the 1900s'), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormolu
abandoned.note: The year of the French legislation; the practice lingered into the 1900s.

Wikipedia, 'Gilding' and 'Ormolu' (fire gilding of copper alloys abandoned for mercury's danger), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilding ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormolu
substrates.note: Oil gilding over the clean bronze is this record's choice for gilt bronze; electroplated gold over nickel is the industrial alternative named by the sources.

surface.burnished: near-mirror: the leaf compressed flat on the bole; roughness has no verified measurement (see unverified)
surface.matte: the leaf follows the fine texture of the gesso or size; a soft, even lustre
surface.texture: leaf seams: faint overlaps at the leaf pitch (80-84 mm) where one leaf lies on the next

photograph: Burnished water gilding is a gold mirror: the room is seen in it, tinted gold, with sharp highlights.
Matte water gilding and oil gilding have a soft, even, warm lustre with no mirror; the two finishes side by side are the gilder's signature.
Faint square seams where one leaf overlaps the next, about 80 mm apart on flat work.
At grazing angles gold whitens toward its edge colour.

evidenceSearch.tier: Gold is calibrated from tier (a): three measured n,k datasets. The bole's colour and the gloss of burnished and matte gilding need a tier (b) specimen: a ColorChecker photograph of a water-gilt test board with burnished, matte and rubbed passages over red bole.

unverified.field: leaf.alloy (silver and copper in 23.75 kt leaf)
unverified.reason: The maker's split of the ~1 % balance between silver and copper was not published on the pages read. A retailer summary quoting '95.2 % gold, 3.6 % silver, 1.2 % copper' for 23 3/4 kt contradicts the carat itself (23.75/24 = 98.96 %) and is rejected.
No measured roughness or gloss of burnished water gilding or oil gilding was read.

The glue-to-water ratio of the gilder's liquor was not found in a source read. Manetti's '1 part glue and 10 parts water' is the rabbit-skin glue for the gesso and the bole (recorded there as glueToWater), not the gilder's liquor.
The 3-hour and 12-hour oil sizes of the trade were not confirmed from a readable source.
No measured reflectance or L*a*b* of a gilder's red bole was read; its albedo needs a tier (b) specimen photograph.
